fields.title: Budapest · Nem beszélek magyarul
fields.context: The language is magyar. “Hungarian” is what the rest of the world calls it.

fields.title: Brussels · Je ne parle pas français
Marseille · Je ne parle pas français
Barcelona · No parlo català
fields.context: Say this and most people switch straight to Spanish or English. Nobody holds it against you.

fields.title: Athens · Δεν μιλάω ελληνικά
fields.context: Δ is a soft th as in this, not a D.

fields.title: Helsinki · En puhu suomea
fields.context: The language is suomi. “Finnish” is what everyone else calls it.

fields.title: Paris · Je ne parle pas français
Helsinki · Anteeksi
fields.groupNote: One word does all three jobs. Finnish doesn’t split them the way Italian or French do.

fields.title: Kraków · Przepraszam
fields.groupNote: One word, three jobs. Polish doesn’t split these the way Italian does.

fields.title: Manchester · Can I get…
fields.context: Manchester minds this far less than London. Can I get passes without comment here.

fields.title: Edinburgh · Could I get…
fields.context: Or “I’ll get” — I’ll get a pint is normal here and would sound abrupt in London.

fields.title: Dublin · Could I get…
fields.context: “Can I get” is the American tell here too, though Dublin minds it considerably less than London does.

fields.title: London · Could I get…
fields.context: “Can I get a coffee” is the American tell. Could I get, or could I have, passes without comment.

fields.title: Brussels · Je voudrais ça
fields.context: Voudrais is the polite conditional. Je veux, “I want,” comes across as blunt.

fields.title: Marseille · Je voudrais ça
fields.context: Voudrais is the polite conditional. Je veux, “I want,” comes across as blunt.

fields.title: Reykjavík · Ég ætla að fá þetta
Oslo · Jeg vil gjerne ha denne
Stockholm · Jag vill gärna ha den här
fields.local: Jag vill gärna ha den här
fields.phonetic: yah vil YAR-nah hah den HAIR

fields.title: Copenhagen · Jeg vil gerne have den her
fields.local: Jeg vil gerne have den her
fields.phonetic: yai vil GER-nuh ha den hair

fields.title: Paris · Je voudrais ça
fields.context: Voudrais is the polite conditional. Je veux, “I want,” comes across as blunt.

fields.title: Zurich · Ich verstah nöd
fields.context: The Swiss version. Ich verstehe nicht is standard German and equally fine.

fields.title: Lisbon · Não percebo
fields.context: Portugal says percebo. Não entendo is the Brazilian phrasing.

fields.title: Lisbon · Queria isto
fields.context: Literally “I would like.” Softer than quero, “I want” — worth the extra syllable.

fields.title: Barcelona · Una taula per a dos
Venice · Vorrei questo
fields.context: Pointing works fine at a bacaro counter. Say it as you point.

fields.title: Munich · Ein Tisch für zwei
fields.context: In beer halls and gardens you share long tables. Ask Ist hier noch frei? (is this seat free?) and sit down.

fields.title: Milan · Un tavolo per due
fields.context: Milan eats dinner around eight, earlier than Rome. Book on Fridays and Saturdays.

fields.title: Warsaw · Stolik dla dwóch osób
fields.context: Literally “a little table for two people.” In milk bars you order at the counter and sit anywhere.

fields.title: Warsaw · Poproszę to
fields.context: Point as you say it. Also works at bakery counters and market stalls.

fields.title: Belfast · Could I get…
fields.context: Can I get passes here without comment. A wee one of anything is also understood.

fields.title: Liverpool · Can I get…
fields.context: Some British people hear “Can I get” as too American. Liverpool barely notices; “Can I have” is the safe version.

fields.title: Glasgow · Could I get…
fields.context: Or just name it — a pint of Tennent’s, please. Glasgow is not fussy about phrasing.

fields.title: Manchester · Sorry
fields.groupNote: Sorry covers both. Excuse me opens a request.

fields.title: Liverpool · Sorry
fields.groupNote: Sorry works for apologising and for getting past. Excuse me is for asking something.

fields.title: Belfast · Sorry
fields.groupNote: Sorry covers both apology and getting past. Excuse me opens a request.

fields.title: Glasgow · Sorry
fields.groupNote: Sorry covers both apology and getting past. Excuse me opens a request.

fields.title: Edinburgh · Sorry
fields.groupNote: Sorry covers apology and getting past. Excuse me opens a request.

fields.title: Dublin · Sorry
fields.groupNote: One word does apology, excuse-me, and getting past. Tone does the distinguishing.

fields.title: London · Sorry
fields.groupNote: One word covers apology, excuse-me, and getting past. Tone does all the distinguishing.

fields.title: Stockholm · Ursäkta
fields.groupNote: Ursäkta covers both getting attention and squeezing past. Förlåt is reserved for an actual apology.

fields.title: Reykjavík · Afsakið
fields.groupNote: One word does both. Fyrirgefðu is kept for a real apology.

fields.title: Oslo · Unnskyld
fields.groupNote: Unnskyld covers both. Beklager is for a genuine apology.

fields.title: Warsaw · Przepraszam
fields.context: On a packed tram, ask Wysiada pan? (vi-SHAH-dah pahn): are you getting off? If not, they let you through.
fields.groupNote: One word for all three. Polish doesn’t split them.
